units.title: Scalars and Variables
units.tip: Scalars are the simplest data type in Perl, holding a single value: a number, string, or reference. You denote a scalar variable with the dollar sign ($) sigil. Understanding scalars is the foundation for everything else in Perl.

lessons.title: The Dollar Sign and Basic Scalars

exercises.question: What sigil denotes a scalar variable in Perl?
exercises.explain: The dollar sign ($) is Perl's scalar sigil. Any variable beginning with $ holds a single scalar value.

exercises.question: Which of these is a valid scalar variable name?
exercises.answer: $name
exercises.explain: $name is a correctly formed scalar variable with the $ sigil followed by a valid identifier.

exercises.question: What does this line do? $x = 42;
exercises.answer: Assigns the number 42 to the scalar variable $x
exercises.explain: The = operator assigns the value on the right (42) to the variable on the left ($x).
choices: Assigns the number 42 to the scalar variable $x
Compares $x to 42 and returns true if equal

exercises.question: What type of value can a Perl scalar hold?
exercises.answer: A number, string, or reference
exercises.explain: A scalar is flexible: it can be a numeric value, a text string, or a reference to another data structure. Perl converts between them as needed.

exercises.question: In Perl, are variable names case-sensitive?
exercises.answer: Yes, $Name and $name are different variables
exercises.explain: Perl treats variable names as case-sensitive, so $Name, $name, and $NAME are three completely separate variables.
choices: Case matters only for special variables

exercises.question: What does $message = "Hello" do with double quotes?
exercises.answer: Assigns the string "Hello" and allows variable interpolation
exercises.explain: Double-quoted strings in Perl interpolate variables, so $var inside them is replaced with its value. Single quotes do not interpolate.
choices: Assigns the string "Hello" and allows variable interpolation

exercises.question: Given $x = 5 and $y = 3, what is the result of $x + $y?
exercises.explain: Perl performs numeric addition on scalar values. 5 + 3 equals 8.

exercises.question: What does $str = "a" . "b" produce?
exercises.answer: The string "ab"
exercises.explain: The dot (.) operator concatenates strings in Perl. "a" . "b" joins them into "ab".

exercises.question: What does undef mean in Perl?
exercises.answer: The absence of a value; undefined state
exercises.explain: undef is Perl's way of saying "no value" or "undefined". A variable that has never been assigned has the value undef.
choices: The absence of a value; undefined state

exercises.question: How do you increment a scalar by 1 in Perl?
exercises.explain: The ++ operator increments a numeric scalar by one. You can also use $x += 1. Both are common in Perl.

units.title: Arrays
units.tip: Arrays are ordered collections of scalars in Perl. The @ sigil denotes an array, while $ accesses individual elements. Arrays start at index 0 and can grow as large as memory allows.

exercises.question: What sigil denotes an array variable in Perl?
exercises.explain: The @ symbol is Perl's array sigil. @array refers to the whole array.

exercises.question: How do you access the first element of @array?
exercises.answer: $array[0]
exercises.explain: Arrays are zero-indexed in Perl. You access a single element with the $ sigil and square brackets, so the first element is $array[0].

exercises.question: What does @colors = ("red", "green", "blue") create?
exercises.answer: An array of three string elements
exercises.explain: This statement creates an array with three strings. Parentheses () group the values, and the comma separates them.
choices: An array of three string elements

exercises.question: How do you get the number of elements in @array?
exercises.answer: scalar(@array) or $#array + 1
exercises.explain: scalar(@array) returns the count of elements. Alternatively, $#array gives the last index, so adding 1 gives the count.

exercises.question: What does $#array represent?
exercises.answer: The index of the last element in the array
exercises.explain: $#array is the last valid index. If an array has 5 elements, $#array is 4 (since indexing starts at 0).
choices: The index of the last element in the array

exercises.question: What does push(@array, "new") do?
exercises.answer: Adds "new" to the end of @array
exercises.explain: push appends one or more elements to the end of an array. It modifies the original array in place.

exercises.question: What does pop(@array) return?
exercises.answer: The last element and removes it from the array
exercises.explain: pop removes and returns the last element of an array. The array is modified.
choices: The last element and removes it from the array

exercises.question: What does splice(@array, 1, 2) do?
exercises.answer: Removes 2 elements starting at index 1
exercises.explain: splice removes and returns elements from an array. splice(array, offset, length) removes length elements starting at offset.
choices: Joins the array into a string

exercises.question: What does @slice = @array[0, 2, 4] do?
exercises.answer: Assigns elements at indices 0, 2, and 4 to @slice
exercises.explain: This is an array slice: it selects multiple elements by index and assigns them to another array.
choices: Assigns elements at indices 0, 2, and 4 to @slice

exercises.question: How do you reverse the order of elements in an array?
exercises.answer: @array = reverse(@array)
exercises.explain: The reverse function reverses the order of array elements. Assigning it back to the array updates it.
choices: No built-in way; you must loop manually

units.title: Hashes
units.tip: Hashes are key-value data structures in Perl, like dictionaries or maps in other languages. The % sigil denotes a hash; use $ to access individual values by key. Hashes are unordered, but each key maps to exactly one scalar value.

exercises.question: What sigil denotes a hash variable in Perl?
exercises.explain: The percent sign (%) is Perl's hash sigil. %hash refers to the entire hash.

exercises.question: How do you access a value in %hash by key?
exercises.answer: $hash{key}
exercises.explain: Individual hash values use the $ sigil (because you get a scalar) and curly braces {}, so the value for a key is $hash{key}.

exercises.question: What does %person = ("name" => "Alice", "age" => 30) create?
exercises.answer: A hash with two key-value pairs
exercises.explain: The => operator (fat comma) creates a key-value pair. This hash has keys "name" and "age" with their corresponding values.
choices: A hash with two key-value pairs

exercises.question: What does keys(%hash) return?
exercises.answer: A list of all keys in the hash
exercises.explain: keys returns a list of all the keys in a hash (in no particular order, since hashes are unordered).
choices: A list of all keys in the hash

exercises.question: What does values(%hash) return?
exercises.answer: A list of all values in the hash
exercises.explain: values returns a list of all the values in a hash (in the same arbitrary order as keys, since hashes are unordered).
choices: A list of all values in the hash

exercises.question: How do you check if a key exists in %hash?
exercises.answer: exists($hash{key})
exercises.explain: The exists function returns true if the key is present in the hash, regardless of whether its value is defined.

exercises.question: What does delete($hash{key}) do?
exercises.answer: Removes the key-value pair from the hash
exercises.explain: delete removes a key and its associated value from the hash. The key no longer exists after deletion.
choices: Removes the key-value pair from the hash
Returns the deleted value (nothing happens to the hash)

exercises.question: What does this loop do? while (my ($k, $v) = each %hash) { print "$k: $v\n" }
exercises.answer: Iterates over key-value pairs and prints each one
exercises.explain: each returns the next key-value pair each time it is called. The while loop continues until each returns no more pairs.
choices: Iterates over key-value pairs and prints each one

exercises.question: How do you get the number of keys in %hash?
exercises.answer: scalar(keys %hash)
exercises.explain: keys in scalar context returns the count of keys. You can also use scalar(values %hash).

exercises.question: What does %empty = (); do?
exercises.answer: Creates an empty hash
exercises.explain: Assigning an empty list () to a hash creates or clears it. All keys and values are removed.

units.title: Context: Scalar vs List
units.tip: Context in Perl determines how an expression is evaluated. Scalar context expects a single value; list context expects zero or more values. The same expression can return different results depending on context. Understanding context is crucial to mastering Perl.

exercises.question: What is scalar context in Perl?
exercises.answer: An evaluation that expects a single scalar value
exercises.explain: Scalar context occurs when an expression is used where one value is expected, like in an assignment to a scalar or a comparison.
choices: An evaluation that expects a single scalar value
An evaluation that expects an array
An evaluation that expects a hash

exercises.question: What is list context in Perl?
exercises.answer: An evaluation that expects zero or more values
exercises.explain: List context occurs when an expression is used where a list is expected, like in an assignment to an array or in a function that wants multiple values.
choices: An evaluation that only expects numbers
An evaluation that expects zero or more values
An evaluation that only expects strings

exercises.question: What does @array in scalar context return?
exercises.answer: The number of elements in the array
exercises.explain: When you use @array where a scalar is expected, Perl returns the array's length, not the array itself.
choices: The number of elements in the array

exercises.question: What does if (%hash) { } test?
exercises.answer: Whether the hash has at least one key
exercises.explain: A hash in boolean context is true when it holds at least one key and false when it is empty.
choices: Whether the hash is a reference
Whether the hash has at least one key

exercises.question: In this line, what context is @colors? @colors = split(/,/, $string)
exercises.answer: List context; it receives the list of split values
exercises.explain: split returns a list of values. The assignment to @colors happens in list context, so @colors receives all the split results.
choices: Scalar context; it receives one value
List context; it receives the list of split values

exercises.question: What does $count = @array; do?
exercises.answer: Assigns the number of elements to $count
exercises.explain: This is scalar context. @array in scalar context evaluates to the array's element count.
choices: Assigns the number of elements to $count

exercises.question: What does ($first, $second) = @array; do?
exercises.answer: Assigns the first two elements to the two variables
exercises.explain: This is list context. @array returns its elements as a list, which are assigned to the scalar variables in order.
choices: Assigns the entire array to both variables
An error (can't assign array to scalars)
Assigns the first two elements to the two variables

exercises.question: What does scalar(keys %hash) do?
exercises.answer: Forces keys to return in scalar context, counting the keys
exercises.explain: keys in list context returns all keys. Wrapping it in scalar() forces scalar context, which returns the count.
choices: Forces keys to return in scalar context, counting the keys
Returns the keys as a string

exercises.question: In this snippet, what context is split()? if (split(/ /, $line) > 3) { }
exercises.answer: Scalar context; it returns the number of parts
exercises.explain: split is used in a numeric comparison (> 3), which forces scalar context. In scalar context split returns the number of fields.
choices: List context; it returns all parts
Scalar context; it returns the number of parts

exercises.question: What does my @copy = @original; do in list context?
exercises.answer: Copies all elements from @original to @copy
exercises.explain: This is list context. @original returns all its elements, which are assigned to @copy. Both arrays are now separate copies.

units.title: Control Flow
units.tip: Control flow statements like if, while, for, and foreach direct how a program executes. They let you repeat code, make decisions, and skip sections based on conditions. Perl supports both C-style loops and array iteration.

exercises.question: What does if ($x > 5) { print "big"; } do?
exercises.answer: Prints "big" only if $x is greater than 5
exercises.explain: The if statement evaluates the condition. If true, the block executes. If false, the block is skipped.
choices: Prints "big" only if $x is greater than 5

exercises.question: What does unless ($error) { proceed(); } do?
exercises.answer: Calls proceed() only if $error is false
exercises.explain: unless is the opposite of if. The block executes when the condition is false (not true).
choices: Calls proceed() only if $error is false

exercises.question: What does while ($i < 10) { print $i; $i++; } do?
exercises.answer: Prints 0 through 9
exercises.explain: The while loop repeats as long as the condition is true. Each iteration, $i is printed then incremented until $i is no longer less than 10.

exercises.question: What does until ($done) { work(); } do?
exercises.answer: Repeats until $done becomes true
exercises.explain: until is the opposite of while. The loop continues as long as the condition is false, and exits when it becomes true.

exercises.question: What does for (my $i = 0; $i < 5; $i++) { print $i; } do?
exercises.answer: Prints 0, 1, 2, 3, 4
exercises.explain: The C-style for loop has three parts: initialize ($i = 0), condition ($i < 5), and increment ($i++). It loops while the condition is true.

exercises.question: What does foreach $item (@list) { print $item; } do?
exercises.answer: Iterates over each element in @list and prints it
exercises.explain: foreach loops over each element of an array. Each iteration, $item holds the current element.
choices: Prints the entire array as one string
Prints the index of each element
Iterates over each element in @list and prints it

exercises.question: What does last; do inside a loop?
exercises.answer: Exits the loop immediately
exercises.explain: last is Perl's equivalent of break in other languages. It exits the innermost loop immediately.

exercises.question: What does next; do inside a loop?
exercises.answer: Skips to the next iteration
exercises.explain: next is Perl's equivalent of continue in other languages. It skips the rest of the current iteration and goes to the next one.

exercises.question: What does redo; do inside a loop?
exercises.answer: Restarts the current iteration without re-evaluating the condition
exercises.explain: redo jumps back to the beginning of the loop block without re-evaluating the loop condition. It is rarely used.
choices: Restarts the current iteration without re-evaluating the condition

exercises.question: What does elsif in an if statement do?
exercises.answer: Provides an additional condition if the previous if is false
exercises.explain: elsif (not else if) tests another condition if the first if was false. You can chain multiple elsif blocks.
choices: Provides an additional condition if the previous if is false

units.title: Subroutines, Regular Expressions, and File I/O
units.tip: Subroutines are reusable code blocks that accept arguments and return values. Regular expressions are patterns for matching and transforming text. File I/O lets you read from and write to files. These advanced features combine into powerful Perl idioms.

exercises.question: What does the =~ operator do in Perl?
exercises.answer: Matches a string against a regular expression
exercises.explain: =~ applies a regex match to a string. It returns true if the pattern matches and false otherwise.
choices: Matches a string against a regular expression

exercises.question: What does if ($str =~ /hello/) { } do?
exercises.answer: Executes the block if $str contains "hello"
exercises.explain: The regex /hello/ is a literal match. It succeeds if "hello" appears anywhere in $str.

exercises.question: What does @matches = $str =~ /(\w+)/g; do?
exercises.answer: Extracts all word sequences from $str into @matches
exercises.explain: The /g flag means global: find all matches. (\w+) captures one or more word characters. Each match is added to @matches.
choices: Extracts all word sequences from $str into @matches

exercises.question: What does open(my $fh, "<", "file.txt") do?
exercises.answer: Opens file.txt for reading
exercises.explain: open associates a filehandle ($fh) with a file. "<" means read mode. You can then read from $fh.

exercises.question: What does while (my $line = <$fh>) { } do?
exercises.answer: Reads lines from the filehandle one at a time
exercises.explain: <$fh> reads the next line from the filehandle. The while loop repeats until no more lines are available (EOF).
choices: Reads the entire file into a single line
Reads lines from the filehandle one at a time

exercises.question: How do you define a subroutine in Perl?
exercises.answer: sub name { code }
exercises.explain: The sub keyword defines a subroutine. Give it a name and a code block. You can call it later with name().

exercises.question: How do you pass arguments to a subroutine?
exercises.answer: Arguments arrive in @_, accessed via $_[0], $_[1], etc.
exercises.explain: When you call a subroutine, Perl places all arguments in the special array @_. You extract them by index.
choices: Arguments arrive in @_, accessed via $_[0], $_[1], etc.

exercises.question: What does return $value; do in a subroutine?
exercises.answer: Exits the subroutine and sends $value back to the caller
exercises.explain: return exits the subroutine and specifies what value the caller receives. Without return, the last expression evaluated is returned.
choices: Exits the subroutine and sends $value back to the caller

exercises.question: What does chomp($line); do?
exercises.answer: Removes the trailing newline from $line
exercises.explain: chomp strips the trailing newline character (\n). This is essential after reading lines from a file.

exercises.question: What does my $var = shift @_; do in a subroutine?
exercises.answer: Removes the first argument from @_ and stores it in $var
exercises.explain: shift removes and returns the first element of an array. In a subroutine, it is commonly used to extract the first argument.
choices: Removes the first argument from @_ and stores it in $var
